item.title: An 80-Cent Plastic Pouch Is Saving Thousands of Women From Dying in Childbirth
item.description:
A few hours after she nearly bled to death, Husaina Balarabe was serenely unaware that her life had been in peril.

She cuddled her newborn baby, a lush-cheeked boy she had named Aabid, and showed him off to her sisters from her bed in a noisy hospital delivery ward in the northern Nigerian city of Kano.

Ms. Balarabe, a 26-year-old optometrist, had experienced a postpartum hemorrhage, a side effect of childbirth that is the leading cause of maternal death around the world.

She did not die because her midwife used a low-cost, low-tech intervention that was pioneered here and in other maternity wards in some of Africa’s poorest places, and that is now saving lives across the continent.

The device was a piece of thin, green plastic the size of a cookie sheet with a pouch at its end, called a maternal drape. It lay beneath Ms. Balarabe as she delivered, and the pouch hung off the end of the bed. The midwife who caught baby Aabid saw blood running into the pouch and quickly reaching and surpassing the danger level — 300 milliliters (or 10 ounces), indicated by a mark on the pouch

The nurse swiftly grabbed a cart stationed in the middle of the packed maternity ward, called for help and went to work. From the cart, she took a syringe of the drug oxytocin and injected it through an IV to get Ms. Balarabe’s uterus to contract. She added a dose of tranexamic acid, to prompt clotting. She massaged Ms. Balarabe’s abdomen, encouraging more uterine contractions, while another nurse started IV fluids to restore her blood volume. The bleeding slowed, and after a couple of minutes, it stopped altogether.

It was all so swift and smooth that the new mother had no idea there was cause for alarm.

One in every 10 women who give birth experiences postpartum hemorrhage, and at least 70,000 women die from it each year. Almost all of those women are in low-income countries; more women die giving birth in Nigeria than in any other country.

Maternal mortality is one of the most bedeviling problems in global health because — until recently — the main solutions have required skilled health care personnel to identify women at risk and to intervene swiftly when a delivery suddenly becomes dangerous. But there is no cheap or simple way to produce midwives and obstetricians, or to convince them to stay in underserved rural areas when they could earn more in cities or other countries.

Postpartum hemorrhage occurs after a baby is born, when the placenta separates from the mother’s body, leaving hundreds of blood vessels open and pumping blood. In a normal delivery, the uterus quickly contracts, and the pressure closes those vessels. But if that contraction doesn’t occur or happens too slowly, or if pieces of the placenta are left behind, blood pours out without stopping, and the woman can die in as little as 10 minutes.

Some bleeding is normal in childbirth. The reason many women die is that it is surprisingly difficult to tell if someone is losing too much blood. Research found that even midwives and doctors who have delivered hundreds of babies consistently underestimate how much blood a woman has lost.

“The amount of blood on the couch, on the floor, on the pads, on my clothes, on her clothes, is it 300 or 500 or 1000 milliliters ?” asked Dr. Hadiza Galadanci, a professor of obstetrics and gynecology at Bayero University in Kano who oversaw the Nigerian research into use of the drape. “A lot of times, we don’t realize the amount of blood that a woman has lost because we make a visual assessment and it’s very, very subjective.”

By the time those delivering a baby decide it’s time to act, it’s often too late.

The drape is now being rolled out across Nigeria. But it was only the first part of the intervention that saved Ms. Balarabe. Next came the series of treatments after the pouch became dangerously full of blood. None of those steps are new, but a few years ago, researchers tested what happened when they were all done at once — massage, oxytocin, tranexamic acid, IV fluids — and quickly. They found that, together with the drape, these interventions cut deaths from postpartum hemorrhage in hospitals by about two-thirds.

Previously, health workers had been trained to respond by first trying massage and then waiting 20 minutes to see if bleeding stopped. If it didn’t, they tried a drug and waited 20 more.

When all the interventions are done together, in what is called a “bundle,” bleeding stops quickly in most women. “It’s like turning off a tap,” Dr. Galadanci said.

If it doesn’t stop, the last step is escalation: getting the woman into an operating room or transferring her to a facility that has staff who can stop the bleeding surgically.

“We have not had one death from postpartum hemorrhage since we started this,” said Binta Garba, who has been the head nurse in the labor ward at Aminu Kano Teaching Hospital for seven years.

Eight or nine times each week, one of her nurses will spot a pouch with blood past the 300-millileter mark and shout, “Bring the bundle!” The person closest to the trolley wheels it to the bedside. “Everybody helps, and in a short period, the bleeding stops,” Ms. Garba said.

When Dr. Galadanci was recruited to be part of this research five years ago, she was skeptical: How could a flimsy sheet of plastic and a small procedural change in treatment save women’s lives? The research convinced her — and she went on a campaign to persuade Nigeria’s health minister to make this the national standard of care.

Now, pairs of midwife-trainers are visiting labor wards across the country to introduce the drape and the bundle. Often, they’re greeted with the same skepticism.

“I thought, We already give oxytocin and tranexamic acid, women still die — you’re wasting my time telling me about something we already do,” Kursiyya Shuaibu, one of the trainers, said of the first time she heard about the new procedure. Then she used it, and saved a woman’s life. “When you bundle it, it’s magic!”

Postpartum hemorrhage also occurs in high-income countries, but women are much less likely to die. They typically have one-on-one care from a midwife or nurse, as well as electronic monitoring of vital signs that can flag a problem early, and blood supply for transfusion is readily available.

Nigeria has high rates of severe postpartum hemorrhage because it has weak primary care. Sixty percent of women are anemic, and there is limited access to birth control. The average woman in the north has seven children, and her risk of hemorrhage rises with each pregnancy.

A quarter of Nigerian women never receive any prenatal care during pregnancy; less than half manage four visits. There is a critical shortage of health care workers throughout the system, from midwives who might screen for high-risk pregnancies to obstetricians who could safely deliver them.

Dr. Galadanci talks fast, walks faster and bristles with impatience to improve the care women receive. She believes the solutions to these basic problems have to be equally simple.

“The drape is not an A.I. thing — it’s the absolute opposite: It’s a simple, simple, intervention that can solve our problems,” she said. “You don’t need a surgeon to come and save a woman. Or to teach you how to do a technique with something you have to buy from outside the country. No. You just need a plastic calibrated drape, and you have your drugs. And it’s done.”

The drape can only do so much, of course: The critical levels of understaffing still put women at risk. On a recent afternoon in the maternity ward at the teaching hospital — the best public hospital in Kano — one woman lost 600 milliliters of blood before anyone intervened. Another woman’s drape went unchecked for nearly 45 minutes after her baby was born.

The drapes used for the research in Nigeria were imported from India, and cost about $3 each. That was more than the national health budget could afford.

Dr. Muhammad Ali Pate, the health minister, wants Nigeria to make more of what it needs. So Dr. Galadanci and her team got in touch with a family-run plastic manufacturer in Kano that made plates, forks and containers for things like vegetable oil. Dr. Galadanci showed the chief engineer a drape: Could they make that?

The company made a prototype, but it was clear that any significant production would require custom-built machinery, which it would need to import from Taiwan. The Gates Foundation, which had helped fund the drape research, was eager to scale up the drape’s use, and offered a $600,000 grant. (The foundation has also backed companies in Kenya and South Africa, where the drape was tested, to manufacture them.)

In exchange, the company, Systs Engineering, agreed to sell the drapes for 70 cents each to the national health system. The war in Iran has since pushed up the cost of raw materials, so these days, the drapes cost 80 cents. The company is making them for all of Nigeria, and it has started to export to some neighboring countries.

Dr. Galadanci has now moved on to the next problem: The drape and the bundle are working well in hospitals, but 60 percent of Nigerian women give birth at home. Her research team is testing a kit for community health workers who attend home births. It has an absorbent mat, and when that fills to the corners, it’s a sign a woman cannot lose any more blood and must be taken to a hospital. The kit also contains the drug misoprostol, which causes the uterus to contract, helping to stop bleeding long enough to get a woman to medical care.

Still, the hospitals are strained. On a recent morning at a maternity clinic in the center of Kano, seven women gave birth in the space of a couple of hours. The lone obstetrician, Dr. Halima Ibrahim, had three urgent cases waiting for cesareans, and a lone midwife oversaw the delivery ward. One woman was whimpering through the contractions of her 11th delivery, while in the corner, a couple of student nurses used the flashlight from a phone to stitch another woman’s episiotomy.

But the drape helps. “It used to be that we lost a woman every month: You are left holding the baby, and the mother is gone,” Dr. Ibrahim said. “Not any more.”

This article is by far my favorite piece of news today. How wonderful that a simple, inexpensive item can save the lives of so many mothers. Dr. Galadanci is a miracle worker. The article also gives me hope that other major societal problems can and will be solved. Thank you for running this piece.

thank you for reading! We have a whole series of stories coming on low-tech low cost interventions making a big difference in maternal mortality – stay with us, as the podcasts say!

This is a great story and much needed reporting that has impacts far beyond a the countries now implementing this method. I worked on an ambulance for years, and every EMT and Paramedic are taught to gauge blood loss by estimating blood loss on the packing material or sheet, which is very inexact, having this drape available for vaginal bleeding, even non-pregnancy related ones, would jump start when the medications are delivered. Many ambulance or medical flights are hours long.

that's so interesting – that you had that experience as an EMT. One of my favorite things that I saw reporting (but alas could not squeeze into the story) was the quiz that the trainers use with midwives and nurses when they are introducing the drape and bundle. Of course the veteran staffers doubt that they have anything new to learn about catching babies – but the trainers show them a series of bowls containing blood; blood-soaked clothing; blood-soaked gauze and pads etc. and ask them to guess how much is in each bowl. In every case it's more blood than a woman can safely lose – but almost no one ever guesses the amounts accurately. They consistently underestimate. It's just really hard to do!

The article touches on this only briefly, but even the best interventions are only as valuable as the team that consistently implements them. When the clinical team found out that a woman had waited 45 minutes before her drape was checked, did they do a debrief, identify the failure points, and make an action plan to prevent it from happening again? The protocols, procedures, steps, and quality assurance components are absolutely vital, every time.

Hi Liz. Great point. It won't surprise you that no, there was no debrief after the 45 minute delay – I'm not sure anyone else noticed it (I was timing, out of curiosity). There were 2 nurses working in a ward of 20 women in active labor. At one point that week, I saw the security guard pulled in to help catch a baby (she seemed pretty skilled.) The gaps that occur reflect the very low level of skilled human resources available, and that requires a long term fix. Thanks for reading.

item.title: U.K. Supreme Court to Hear Challenge to Ban on Palestine Action: What to Know
item.description:
Britain’s decision to outlaw Palestine Action, a pro-Palestinian direct-action group, as a terrorist organization has been challenged in a succession of legal hearings since it was imposed last year. Now, the country’s Supreme Court is set to hear a challenge against the ban and decide its future.

The British government accused Palestine Action of orchestrating “a nationwide campaign of direct criminal action,” putting national security at risk. According to the government’s independent adviser on counterterrorism legislation, it was the first time a protest group that did not call for violence against people was proscribed under counterterrorism laws.

Here’s what to know.

Palestine Action was founded in 2020 as a pro-Palestinian protest group that largely focuses its efforts on demonstrations against corporate and military targets linked to the sale and export of defense equipment to Israel. The group says it does not promote violence against individuals.

It was co-founded by Huda Ammori, an advocate who had previously worked for a Palestinian rights organization, and Richard Barnard, an activist linked with other grass roots movements, including Extinction Rebellion, a global environmental group.

During legal proceedings challenging the ban, Britain’s High Court said that the group claimed to have a mailing list of some 20,000 people but that the “extent and nature” of Palestine Action’s membership and organization was “largely unexplained.” Analysts said that before it was disbanded, Palestine Action was run by a relatively small, committed group of activists.

The group’s actions have drawn international attention. President Trump criticized it after activists were accused of vandalizing one of his Scottish golf resorts by defacing the clubhouse and spraying “Gaza is not 4 sale” across a green. Mr. Trump called the demonstrators “terrorists” and said he hoped they would be “treated harshly.”

The Terrorism Act 2000, introduced under a previous Labour prime minister, Tony Blair, allows the government to ban any group “concerned in terrorism.” It contains a broad definition of terrorism that includes damage to property, not just people, if it is carried out for ideological reasons.

The British government announced its plan to designate Palestine Action a terrorist group in June 2025, three days after some of its members damaged military planes using red paint at Britain’s largest air force base, at Brize Norton in Oxfordshire. Yvette Cooper, then the home secretary, said the group’s activities met the legal definition of terrorism because they included “serious damage to property.”

The ban was imposed in July, and the group was added to the statutory list of more than 80 banned terrorist organizations, alongside the Islamic State, Al Qaeda, and Atomwaffen Division, a white supremacist group. At the time, Palestine Action said it was “plainly preposterous” to group it with such organizations.

The ban made it a criminal offense to belong to Palestine Action, express an opinion or belief in support of the group, or wear clothing or carry items that “arouse reasonable suspicion that the individual is a member or supporter” of the group, among other actions. The maximum penalty for belonging to or expressing support for the group is 14 years in prison.

In August, the United States followed suit, designating Palestine Action as a terrorist group.

More than 4,000 people had been arrested across Britain for showing support for the group as of Nov. 1, according to Defend Our Juries, a civil liberties group. Between Sept. 11, 2001, and March 31, 2025, there were a total of 5,734 terrorism arrests in Britain.

The arrests related to Palestine Action stemmed largely from coordinated demonstrations, analysts say, where some protesters have deliberately risked detention by holding placards reading: “I oppose genocide, I support Palestine Action.” Hundreds of people were detained over the weekend outside the U.S. Embassy in London after staging such a protest.

Some civil liberties organizations argue that using counterterrorism legislation against Palestine Action is overreach and part of a wider crackdown on protest in Britain. They contend that existing criminal laws cover property destruction, whereas proscription criminalizes anyone expressing moral support for the proscribed group, including by attending peaceful gatherings.

In July 2025, the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, Volker Türk, called the move a “disproportionate and unnecessary” expansion of counterterrorism powers and called on the British government to rescind its decision.

In written submissions to the Supreme Court, Amnesty International and Liberty argue that the proscription of Palestine Action has silenced broad segments of civil society, academics, journalists and even their own human rights organizations.

David Mead, a human rights law scholar at the University of East Anglia, said the central legal dispute turns on whether the ban is proportionate.

“The surprising thing is the U.K. state’s seeming need to use terrorism legislation on a group such as this,” Professor Mead said.

Ms. Ammori, the co-founder, first challenged the ban in June 2025, and the case has since wound its way through the legal system. In February, the High Court ruled the ban unlawful, calling it disproportionate and an infringement on fundamental rights to free expression and assembly.

That decision was overturned in June by the Court of Appeal. Ms. Ammori appealed that ruling, sending the case to the Supreme Court for what will be the final word in British domestic courts.

Supreme Court rulings are usually issued in three to six months, but legal analysts said the court could rule sooner in this case as hundreds of people arrested and charged in relation to protests are awaiting trial.

Ms. Ammori has said that if the Supreme Court upholds the ban, she plans to take the case to the European Court of Human Rights.

Stephen Castle, Lizzie Dearden and Michael Shear contributed to this report

item.title: Could a Viral Video Save Her Mom’s Chinese Restaurant?
item.description:
Sophie Li wiped the tables and swept the floors every day at China Star, even though few customers came through the door.

For nearly 20 years, Mrs. Li’s Chinese restaurant in Edinburgh has been both her life’s work and her cross to bear. In better times, business was steady enough to support her and her two daughters and help send them to universities.

But early this year, the restaurant was almost always empty. Still, Mrs. Li, approaching 70, scrimped and toiled seven days a week to keep China Star open.

“I am a person who can endure hardship better than humiliation,” she said.

Down in London, her younger daughter, Lisa He, worried about the toll on her mother’s health. She traveled up to Scotland and posted a plea on social media.

“My mum’s Chinese restaurant is dying,” Ms. He, 29, said in a video on Instagram in April. She had decided to put aside several months to try to save it.

“Follow the journey and let’s see if I can turn this around,” she said.

Within days, the post had been viewed millions of times. Influencers and sympathetic locals suddenly flocked to China Star, overwhelming the modest 13-table restaurant.

Neither Ms. He nor her mother had been ready for internet stardom. She wondered whether she had made a mistake.

“It was absolutely awful,” Ms. He said. Going viral “doesn’t help when your restaurant’s already broken.”

Sitting in China Star’s dining room can feel like taking a trip back in time.

An aquarium filled with shy fish welcomes diners, and lucky cat figurines sit in the window. Decorations from a long-ago wedding still hang on the back wall. Dishes are washed by hand.

Mrs. Li was born Wei Li but took the name Sophie after emigrating to Edinburgh in 1993 from mainland China with her husband, a doctoral candidate at the University of Edinburgh. She liked the regal sound of her new name, and hoped to live up to it. To support the family, she worked as a dishwasher and waited tables.

But she didn’t feel at ease in her new home. She worried that Lisa and her older sister, Emma, would not assimilate. In 1997, with loans from relatives and friends, she opened a restaurant, then a decade later moved to her current location, on busy West Maitland Street, beneath a large red sign with “China Star” in gold letters.

“I felt like my standing wasn’t as high when I first came,” she said. She wanted her children “to hold their head high.”

Her chefs were from Hong Kong and southern China, and they cooked a version of Chinese food that had been shaped in postwar Britain into a cuisine of its own: salt-and-pepper stir-fries, sweet and sour chicken, fried noodles and curries. Mrs. Li eventually kept two menus: one for Chinese visitors and one for locals.

She worked 15-hour days, sleeping only a few hours per night. Mornings were for cleaning and ingredient prep. Then came lunch service. She waited tables and delivered takeout orders herself, keeping the restaurant open until midnight, even on Christmas.

Time passed. Her husband returned to China. Her daughters moved to London. Mrs. Li paid off the mortgage on China Star.

But as newer Chinese restaurants opened in Edinburgh and competition grew, the restaurant began to feel more like a burden. Foot traffic ebbed, and more of her business shifted to internet orders, whose commissions ate into their margins. Online ratings for the restaurant dropped.

Mrs. Li does not consider herself tech-savvy, so she didn’t see the customer reviews that complained about small portion sizes or bland fried rice. Arthritis was slowing her down. And she felt lonely.

“I didn’t think there was much hope,” she said. “But I had to keep going. There’s no other road to walk.”

In London, Ms. He, who was making a living as an actress and paralegal, kept tabs on China Star by logging into its CCTV camera. She saw how tired her mother looked. Early this year, she booked a trip home, hoping to give her a break.

“I came back out of a desperation to save my mom, rather than save the restaurant,” she said.

Ms. He has complicated feelings about restaurant life. When she was a baby, her mother brought her to work, putting her in a makeshift crib in a side room. After school, she felt guilty watching her work so hard.

“I often felt like I had to give up my social life to help out at the restaurant,” she said.

Before April, Ms. He’s social media account consisted mostly of images of her dancing or in film rehearsals.

But in this video, she turned the camera on her mother and China Star and gave her own, raw assessment of something many businesses may prefer to hide: what wasn’t working, from the uninviting facade to the outdated menu. And she invited people to follow her own journey as she tried to turn their fortunes around.

Perhaps it was Ms. He’s candor, or the video’s documentary style. Or perhaps it was the feeling, for watchers online, that they could still stave off the loss of yet another family-run business in a world of corporations and chains.

Ms. He’s comments lit up with offers of help, from improving the design to revamping the menu. Diners promised to visit. Restaurant owners encouraged them to rethink the business. “Don’t give up,” one said. “It isn’t over until it’s over.”

Ms. He posted the video on a Sunday. On Tuesday, she found herself back in the kitchen, trying to manage a situation for which they were entirely unprepared.

Food bloggers and new diners filled the restaurant in the days after that viral post. Mrs. Li, who learned of her daughter’s post only after it blew up, was shocked.

Suddenly, daughter and mother were racing up and down stairs to take orders as their two cooks, used to a scattering of orders each day, suddenly had to pump out dishes.

Tensions boiled over when one frustrated chef walked out in protest during lunch as a full house waited for meals. Overwhelmed, the mother and daughter decided to shutter the restaurant temporarily.

People following China Star’s struggles online replied to Ms. He with thoughts about what the restaurant needed to survive, and she decided to act on some of the advice.

She convinced her mother to slim down the menu and add Chinese wines, hired more servers and installed an electronic system for orders. They reopened after about a week with earlier hours and they closed on Mondays.

She shared updates on Instagram, where more than 200,000 accounts are now following her.

Five months after going viral, Ms. He was still working in the dining room, taking orders and mixing drinks. On a Thursday this September, the tables were filled with people who had seen her videos, drawn as much by the story of filial devotion and small-business survival as by the food.

“Usually the second generation — they don’t want to do the restaurant work,” said Wing Cheong, a visitor from Canada. “I think she is a good daughter.”

Mrs. Li, energized, could not imagine giving up China Star, and was hopeful that her daughter would take it over one day. Revenues this summer more than tripled from the year before, and the online attention has led to sponsorships.

But Ms. He wasn’t sure.

She was struggling to balance it all — the social media posts, the long days, the physical labor. There was a leak in the storeroom; a bathroom toilet seat needed fixing.

Beneath it lay a familiar generational dilemma: She had put her own career, and her ambitions to act and dance, on hold to keep her mother’s business afloat.

In one post this summer, she asked whether going viral had made their lives better, or just busier. In her mind, maybe it was time to let China Star go, for her mother to retire and for her to go back to London.

Her video had succeeded. But it had also revealed how differently mother and daughter imagined what should come next.

“If I’m tiring myself and my mom to death every day,” she said at the restaurant, in a quiet moment before lunch, “I don’t really see that as a success.”

For now, decisions on the future would have to wait. For the first time in a long time, the restaurant had large bookings for the holidays in December, and there was plenty of work to do: folding napkins, sorting prawn crackers and washing glasses. They would be back the next day to do it all again.

In April, I saw a video from Lisa He about her mother, and their struggling family-run restaurant. The restaurant, China Star, reminded me of a lot of businesses run by an older generation — once local institutions, but facing closure in an increasingly competitive industry.

item.title: Under Patagonian Spires: Where Pumas, Sheep Herding and Fine Dining Collide
item.description:
As the sun set in the remote south of Patagonia, the jagged shadows of Torres del Paine, the mountains at the heart of Chile’s iconic national park, stretched across the Las Chinas River Valley.

But another drama was playing out in the gloom on the valley floor, where our headlight beams were catching the woolly rumps of sheep as they bumped over tufts of grass.

With whistles and cries, baqueanos — Chile’s version of gauchos, or horseman-herders — hurried the flock across the Patagonian steppe, a wind-torn landscape of rain-soaked logs, wide lakes and lush pastures, toward a corner of the field for the night.

“I never get bored of this,” said Víctor Sharp, one of the baqueanos at Estancia Cerro Guido, the ranch and luxury lodge where I’d booked a three-day stay in early October.

Lighting another cigarette as dusk rolled across the plain, Mr. Sharp took a final lingering look at the mountains before climbing back into his jeep. Behind him, three sheepdogs leaped into the trailer and nestled around the carcass of a sheep, the latest victim of a puma attack.

For more than a century, estancias — the livestock ranches that dot the vast Patagonian wilderness — have played host to a bitter conflict between sheep farmers and pumas. Now, some estancias are awakening to the possibilities of conservation tourism, luring travelers from the backpackers’ trail to a broader experience of Patagonian culture.

Some already offer daylong ranching experiences and rudimentary overnight stays. Estancia Cerro Guido, however, the largest ranch in Chilean Patagonia, sits well ahead of this curve and demonstrates that a working ranch can also offer comfort.

About 65 miles north of Puerto Natales, a tourist town tucked among the fjords, Estancia Cerro Guido sprawls across 264,400 acres of grassland, shimmering azure lakes and snow-dusted peaks in the southern Andes.

In 2019, the Matetic and Simunovic families, two Chilean dynasties of Croatian descent, decided to turn their sprawling Cerro Guido property into something more than just a livestock ranch. While they aimed to maintain sheep and cattle rearing (and the baqueano tradition that came with it), they also wanted livestock to coexist with wildlife and tourism.

Now, two dozen baqueanos manage about 18,600 sheep and 1,800 head of cattle. Meanwhile, a hotel with a new dining area and 21 comfortable rooms cocoons guests from the wildness of the Patagonian weather. And a conservation foundation maintains the delicate balance between wild pumas and livestock.

The hotel’s luxurious, all-inclusive guest experience is almost entirely bespoke. Each evening, the next day’s outings are planned in a glass-walled room off the bar area with the help of a young and enthusiastic staff wearing boinas, or Patagonian berets. An expansive roster of activities immerses visitors in the working life of a ranch and serves as an enviable base from which to visit Torres del Paine National Park.

The other guests and I were made to feel as if we were part of the working ranch while also being regaled with the trappings of comfort and luxury. On a half-day horseback ride, I accompanied the stablehands as they checked in on newborn foals, and then sat down to admire the views with a charcuterie board in the shade of a lenga tree. On the first evening, I helped herd the sheep back to the ranch, before sitting down to a three-course meal.

The list goes on: There are archaeological expeditions to sites where arrowheads and weapons have been found, and treks across the valley to observe ancient rock art stamped in ocher. One afternoon, when the weather cleared, I hiked up to a rocky outcrop on the Sierra Baguales where, traversing a prehistoric lakebed, I found perfectly preserved segments of petrified wood littering the grasslands.

Later in the season, guests might find themselves helping shear the flock — or, on the conservation tour, checking camera traps or recording traces of pumas across the grasslands. The goal, I learned, is to ensure that visitors, however involved they choose to be, leave with a deeper understanding of Patagonia, its culture and its fragile equilibrium.

It’s a tagline here that Patagonia can offer all four seasons in a single day. The valley that stretches out before the hotel is often mottled by the shadows of clouds, with different parts soaked by rain, battered by hail and bathed in brilliant sunshine. After a day out in the elements, I whiled away my evenings watching the weather drift across the pampa from a cozy seat at the bar, or in the restaurant run by Claudio Fourcade, the hotel’s effervescent head chef.

After moving to Modena, Italy, in 2019, Mr. Fourcade discovered a love of curing meats and cooking on an open flame — two cornerstones of Patagonian cuisine. When the offer to join Cerro Guido came in 2023, it was a “match made in heaven,” he said.

“Our mission is to rescue the culinary traditions of ranch culture, with techniques like smoking, salting and fermentation,” he explained.

Mr. Fourcade and his team grow their fruit and root vegetables on the grounds; a greenhouse houses herbs, tomatoes and sprays of edible flowers for garnish. The smoky flavors are nurtured in a tiny smoking cabin behind the kitchen. Every evening, Mr. Fourcade feeds fruitwood into a burner that pipes fragrant smoke over the lines of bondiola, chistorra and prosciutto that hang in the dark.

The results are spectacular, and the three-course lunch and dinner menus change every day. During my stay, lentil and smoked sausage soup was served with heavy, flame-grilled churrasca bread, red pepper salsa and butter creamed with a shot of espresso and a sprinkling of matcha. For lunch on my first full day on the ranch, as I watched a spring storm batter the Sierra del Cazador on the far side of the valley, I was kept warm by pulmay, an arrangement of smoked sausage, fish, clams and pork in a salty broth. At another meal, lamb chops were accompanied by star-anise-infused carrot pickle, and honeyed, smoked pork ribs that held together just long enough to be loaded onto my fork.

Biodynamic wines from the Matetic family vineyards are paired with each course, and fruit from the cassis, red currant and sarsaparilla plants forms the base of the many inventive cocktails. On Wednesday and Sunday evenings, there’s a buffet dinner with barbecued meats and spit-roasted lamb, a Patagonian staple.

When sheep were introduced to Patagonia in the late 19th century, they immediately thrived. With the British textile industry’s thirst for raw materials, estancias popped up across the steppe to capitalize on demand. By the 1920s, there were about two million sheep across the region’s pastures.

But an inevitable conflict arose. Southern Chile is the kingdom of the Patagonian puma (Puma concolor), the apex predator on the steppe. Estancias, at risk of losing 10 percent of the flock each year to puma attacks, employed leoneros, professional bounty hunters, to hunt them. (Until the 1980s, it was legal to hunt puma in Chile.)

“I knew Cerro Guido as an iconic estancia, but one where more than 80 pumas were killed every year,” said Pía Vergara, the founder and director of the Cerro Guido Conservation Foundation.

Ms. Vergara’s conservation project was incorporated into the estancia’s operations in 2019. Her foundation has trained 25 Maremma mountain dogs to live among the flocks and bark to ward off predators. Before long, puma attacks were down 51 percent. Neighboring estancias noticed, and have since purchased and trained their own dogs.

Since 2021, all guests have been invited on a half-day conservation tour as part of their hotel package. Shortly after arriving, I jumped into a jeep with two other guests and was handed a pair of binoculars as we headed out to the condorera, or condor’s roost, a 5,000-acre conservation area. The heads of sandy-brown guanacos, llama-like herbivores, protruded from among the thorny calafate bushes.

Not all guests spot pumas on their tours; none appeared for us. But the tantalizing prospect of seeing one of the elusive animals kept me and my fellow guests intently focused on the landscape. And as recompense, we saw other wildlife — including a ñandú, a flightless bird similar to an ostrich, as well as condors and eagles.

“We want to demonstrate as a foundation that it’s possible to do tourism in a respectful, responsible way,” said Ms. Vergara, who came to Patagonia five times herself before seeing her first puma.

The alternative, she explained, is an “extractive” form of tourism — in which you arrive somewhere and “do whatever you can to get your puma photo,” she said. “We want to show people how and why we are protecting these species.”

When I made it back from the conservation tour, I scraped the mud from my boots, ordered a glass of Baguales whiskey and, listening to hail tap against the wide window at the front of the bar, reflected on my time at Cerro Guido.

So far, I’d tried to track pumas (without great success), herded sheep, survived bursts of driving rain, ridden a jeep down muddy tracks and enjoyed three-course meals. What’s more, I had learned about the extreme fragility of this landscape and the urgent need to protect it.

It felt like I’d condensed Patagonian ranch life into a day. It felt like the new face of Patagonian tourism.

item.title: Senji Kuroi Has Died. He Interpreted ‘the Salaried Soul.’
item.description:
Senji Kuroi, the Japanese novelist and essayist who chronicled the anxieties of postwar corporate life and the muted emotional landscapes of ordinary, white-collar employees navigating a rapidly modernizing Japan, died on Oct. 12 at 94.

His death, from pneumonia, was widely reported in the Japanese media.

A writer of quiet restraint rather than sweeping flourish, Mr. Kuroi built his reputation on stories that often unfolded in offices, commuter trains and modest homes — spaces where ambition, conformity and private yearning collided in ways that rarely produced dramatic explosions but left deep emotional aftershocks.

Critics frequently described him as an interpreter of “the salaried soul,” capturing the unease that simmered beneath Japan’s economic miracle and the quiet disillusionment that followed it.

Over a career spanning more than half a century, he published dozens of novels, short-story collections and essays, earning major Japanese literary prizes and a devoted readership among those who saw their own anxieties reflected in his characters’ small hesitations and moral compromises.

His prose, spare and attentive, resisted grand pronouncements. Instead, he favored the accumulation of small details — a pause in conversation, the hum of fluorescent lights, a gesture left unfinished — through which entire emotional worlds were revealed.

Though less internationally known than contemporaries like Kenzaburo Oe and Haruki Murakami, Mr. Kuroi was widely regarded in Japan as one of the most perceptive observers of everyday life in the late 20th century.

His work bridged generations. Shaped by the austerity of the postwar years yet skeptical of the corporate conformity that defined the high-growth era, he portrayed individuals who felt quietly estranged from the very prosperity they had helped build.

In a seminal, two-volume survey of Japanese literature, “Dawn to the West” (1984), the literary historian Donald Keene remarked of Mr. Kuroi and the other writers known as the Introspective Generation that their novels and short stories often concerned “the minute observation of everyday existence.”

Critics often noted that Mr. Kuroi’s narratives seemed to revolve around almost nothing — a chance encounter, a memory resurfacing, a minor workplace dispute — yet his fiction revealed how such moments could destabilize a life.

The effect was quietly radical. While Japanese literature was becoming increasingly globalized and experimental, Mr. Kuroi insisted on the value of ordinary experience. He wrote about people who might never appear in headlines: middle managers, aging parents, couples struggling to communicate after decades together.

Literary scholars sometimes placed Mr. Kuroi within the tradition of the shishosetsu, or “I-novel,” a distinctly Japanese form that blurs autobiography and fiction. Yet his work was less confessional than observational. Even when drawing on his own corporate experiences, he maintained a careful distance, allowing readers to project their own uncertainties onto his characters.

Mr. Kuroi’s early novel “Time” (1969) clearly illustrated this approach. The protagonist, not strongly individualized, is a midlevel employee navigating routine office life at a company. The narrative follows his internal reflections as he participates in meetings and commutes between home and the office.

His novel “Life in the Cul-De-Sac” (1984) also demonstrated this technique. The story focuses on neighbors in a suburban housing development. The characters are defined by subtle gestures and fragments of thought rather than dramatic personal histories. The result is a narrative in which the author rarely intrudes, characters remain somewhat opaque and readers supply the emotional interpretation.

“By picking up small things and observing them, something begins to come into view,” Mr. Kuroi explained in a 2017 interview in Sarai magazine.

Senji Kuroi was the pen name for Shunjiro Osabe. He was born on May 28, 1932, in Tokyo. His father, Kingo Osabe, was a prosecutor who became a Supreme Court judge.

The future author came of age during Japan’s postwar reconstruction, when discipline and collective effort were prized above individual expression, even more than it traditionally had been. These experiences would later inform his writing, which often examined the tension between social obligation and personal identity.

As a high school student, Mr. Kuroi engaged in correspondence with the popular postwar novelist Noma Hiroshi about how he, too, could pursue a career in literature. The writer advised Mr. Kuroi to study economics and work in business. “Japanese literature’s hopes are so small,” Mr. Hiroshi reportedly told him, “because there are almost no writers who understand society.”

After graduating in 1955 with an economics degree from the University of Tokyo, Mr. Kuroi joined Fuji Heavy Industries, a major manufacturing company. The routines of office life — endless meetings, carefully calibrated hierarchies, the quiet erosion of personal aspiration — became the raw material for his early fiction.

As a junior executive, or “salary man,” Mr. Kuroi took his pen name in the 1950s when he began publishing short stories and novels while still employed at Fuji, to avoid possible conflicts with his bosses. In 1970, he resigned from Fuji to devote himself full time to writing.

His literary breakthrough came in the late 1960s and early 1970s, when a new generation of Japanese writers turned away from overt political themes toward the psychological consequences of rapid economic growth. Mr. Kuroi’s stories stood out for their precise realism and emotional subtlety.

He was prolific, churning out 25 novels and novellas, dozens of short stories and numerous essay collections. Japanese bibliographies count more than 50 separate volumes of his writing.

Like many Japanese authors, Mr. Kuroi often published fiction first as serialized installments in literary magazines before issuing them as books. That was the case most prominently with “Life in the Cul-De-Sac,” which won the Tanizaki Prize, one of Japan’s most coveted literary awards. Its English translation by Philip Gabriel in 2001 was the first substantial introduction of Mr. Kuroi’s fiction to an American audience.

Younger writers admired Mr. Kuroi’s discipline and clarity and his ability to transform the mundane into something profound. Others noted his refusal to romanticize either tradition or modernity.

Although more translations of his work appeared in English and other languages, his international reputation remained modest. Some translators and critics said that the qualities that made him revered in Japan — subtle tonal shifts, cultural nuances, the weight of social expectations conveyed through small gestures — were difficult to carry across linguistic boundaries.

As Japan’s economic bubble burst in the 1990s and long-held assumptions about lifetime employment began to erode, Mr. Kuroi’s earlier themes took on new resonance. The quiet dissatisfaction he had depicted decades earlier seemed prophetic to some critics, who saw his fiction as an early warning about the emotional costs of conformity.

In later works, his focus broadened to include aging, memory and the fragility of human connections. Characters looked back on careers and relationships with a mixture of regret and acceptance, asking whether the compromises of youth had been necessary or merely habitual.

Mr. Kuroi’s novel “Curtain Call” (1994) reflected the deepening concern in his work for the quiet reckoning that accompanies the later stages of life. The book follows a middle-aged man who begins to look back on the choices and compromises that have shaped his career and personal relationships, gradually sensing the passage of time as both loss and revelation.

An intensely private man, Mr. Kuroi revealed little of his personal life over the years, even to his translators. Information about survivors was not immediately available.

In his interview with Sarai magazine, Mr. Kuroi, then 85, spoke about his determination to remain a productive author.

“Even if it isn’t fiction itself, I want to keep writing something,” he said. But he lamented that writers rarely completed everything they hoped to write. “It is natural for a life to end in the middle of things,” he added.

item.title: John Frieda, Hair-Care Mogul Who Soothed Women’s Curls, Has Died
item.description:
John Frieda, the elegant British hair-care mogul who made his name as a young assistant stylist in Mayfair in the late 1960s, married the Scottish pop star Lulu in the 1970s and then made his fortune in the 1990s by smoothing the locks of curly-haired women with a blockbuster product called Frizz Ease, died on Tuesday in London. He was 75.

The cause of death, at a hospital near his home, was cancer, Gail Federici, his business partner, said.

Mr. Frieda was handsome, reserved and fastidious. He was not given to salon-chair chitchat — he trained his staff never to inquire about a client’s holiday plans — and was possessed of rigorous technical skills. (He had terrific hair, and cut it himself.) He opened his first salon in 1976 in London’s West End, serving the rock stars, aristocrats, actors and artists that made up the jet set of the time: Jackie Kennedy, Mick Jagger, Princess Diana and Diana Ross all graced his chairs.

Shirley MacLaine once sent him a pot plant as a thank-you gift for her distinctive shag. “When I shake my hair,” she wrote on the card, “I display your art.”

Counter to the mores of the times — and to Ms. MacLaine’s thoughtful gift — his salon was not a louche hangout perfumed with the scent of marijuana. It was clean and white and all business.

“Hairdressing had been quite formal,” he told the British Beauty Council, a nonprofit organization, in June 2026. “But the 1960s happened, and the breaking-down of barriers between aristocracy and the working class. In the top salons, the stylists were wearing bell-bottoms with long hair and smoking cigarettes; it was now all very pally. And I thought, ‘No, I don’t want this!’”

Shortly after his salon opened, he heard from the actress Joanna Lumley, who played Purdey, a secret agent with crack martial arts skills on “The New Avengers,” the successor to the original show, which aired for a year starting in 1976. She had seen a photo of a cut and color that Mr. Frieda had done for Vogue; it was a perky bob, and she thought it just right for her character.

“Purdey Mania, the haircut that sweeps Britain,” the tabloids declared, and the salon was booked solid for the next six months.

Mr. Frieda opened another salon in Mayfair in the early 1980s, and went on to open more in New York, Los Angeles and Ibiza, Spain.

We investigate, research and ask around before settling on our subjects. If you know of someone who might be a candidate for a Times obituary, please suggest it here.

In 1988, he got a call from Boots, the British beauty retailer, about doing a line of products. Why not? He had been developing his own styling potions.

He was invited on “Richard & Judy,” a British talk show, where he demonstrated one of those products, a thickening lotion that he had been using in his salon. These were the Big Hair years, and Mr. Frieda was an expert in the genre.

“The switchboard jammed,” he told The Evening Standard in 2001. “Boots sold out. Next thing I get a call, ‘Here’s an order for 1.2 million bottles of thickening lotion and 860,000 jars of wax.’”

He didn’t have a clue how to fulfill such big orders, but happily he had just met Ms. Federici, an American hair-care executive, and they formed a partnership. Ms. Federici, who has wavy hair, also suggested that they create something to tame the frizz of women with curls. Frizz Ease, a silicone-based serum, was their solution. It was so successful that newspapers reported that, at one point, a bottle was being sold every 30 seconds.

“Trade magazines called it the hula hoop,” Ms. Federici said in an interview, “because it just flew out of the stores.”

In 2002, they sold the product business, John Frieda Professional Hair Care, to Kao Corporation, a Japanese company, for $450 million. Mr. Frieda retained ownership of his salons.

“He was such an elegant man and such an innovator,” Linda Wells, the founding editor of Allure magazine, wrote on Instagram after Mr. Frieda’s death. “Frizz Ease alone defined the ’90s. How lucky I was to meet him. The angels are going to have a good hair day.”

Alan Howard Frieda was born on July 5, 1951, in London, one of four children of Hannah Mary (Dochtery) Frieda and Isidore Frieda, who owned a hair salon in Ealing, a neighborhood in West London.

When he was 5, he contracted rheumatic fever and spent a year in the hospital, unable to walk for nine months. Following the tradition of the era, his parents were allowed to visit only on weekends. He was terrified most of the time, he later told The Times of London, speculating that the experience may account for his reserve.

Alan helped out at his father’s salon on Saturdays, but Isidore, the son of a Fleet Street barber who had fled the pogroms in Poland in the late 19th century, wanted his son to be a doctor.

“I became a hairdresser for all the wrong reasons,” Mr. Frieda told The Standard in 2012. “To get out of studying. My father was very angry. But when he realized I was determined, he said I must work for the top salon in London.”

He added: “I probably argued with my father more than anybody, and yet he was the person I loved more than anybody. People would say, ‘Don’t treat your father like that,’ and he’d say, ‘No, I like it when he shouts at me because he gets it out!’”

When he was 16, Alan went to work for Leonard Lewis, otherwise known as Leonard of Mayfair, who was known for giving a young model named Lesley Hornby an Eton crop, as her boyish cut was called — transforming her into Twiggy — and for shearing the heads of the Beatles into their signature mop tops. His first task, on his first day, was folding towels, which he did with the precision that marked his character.

He soon changed his name to John, because there was another Alan at Leonard’s, and stylists, by tradition, go by their first names.

Mr. Lewis noted his new employee’s attention to detail and made Mr. Frieda his assistant on fashion shoots. In the scrum of celebrity, Mr. Frieda met Lulu, the Scottish pop star behind “To Sir With Love” and other hits. When they married in 1976, in a civil service at the Hampstead town hall, Ringo Starr, Tom Jones and Elton John were among the guests who attended the party.

But Mr. Frieda didn’t want to be known as Mr. Lulu, he told The Times. The marriage prompted him to go out on his own. “I would have been humiliated and ashamed for people to think I was living off her,” he said.

The couple divorced in 1991. Mr. Frieda married Avery Agnelli, the widow of the Italian industrialist Giovanni Alberto Agnelli, in 2019; she had been his partner since 2002. She survives him, along with their children, Jackson and Leyla; a son from his first marriage, the actor Jordan Frieda; a stepdaughter, Asia Agnelli Lagrange; two grandchildren; and his brother, Nigel.

Mr. Frieda led a sprawling domestic life, with homes in London and Hampshire, a clutch of properties in Ibiza and a ski lodge in Verbier, Switzerland. He collected works of art by Francis Bacon and Lucian Freud, read Eastern philosophy — he was once a follower of Gurumayi, whose upstate New York ashram was much in vogue in the 1990s — and founded HAIRraising, a charity that benefits pediatric hospitals in Britain and the U.S.

“The harder you work, the luckier you become,” Mr. Frieda told The Times in June. “No matter how charmed someone’s life may seem, you can’t avoid suffering and pain. And you shouldn’t be trying to, because they’re your teachers.”

He added: “I wasn’t really authentic when I was younger. I was trying to look like I knew what I was doing.”

Karla Adam contributed reporting.

item.title: A Trump Reckoning
item.description:
The word “historic” is overused in journalism. But now that we know the results of the U.S. midterms, it feels like the best word to do the moment justice. There were a lot of firsts.

In the end it wasn’t just a blue wave; it was a blue tsunami. (Which may also explain why President Trump told The New York Times on election night that he wouldn’t contest the results.)

The Democrats are poised to control both houses of Congress, making the president, who is heading into the last two years of his second and final term, a particularly hobbled lame duck. Today I write about what that means for America and for the world.

There are multiple ways the U.S. midterm elections made history this week.

A Black woman was elected governor for the first time in U.S. history (in Georgia). Native American women were elected as governor (in New Mexico) and as senator (in Minnesota) for the first time.

America will have its first Muslim senator (from Michigan) and its first openly gay male senator (from New Hampshire). There’s now a former Paralympian in the Senate and the first Gen Z woman in the House.

You’d be forgiven for missing all these, though, because they’ve been overshadowed by the scale of the blue tsunami that just swept through America.

Texas — where Elon Musk spent hundreds of millions of dollars supporting the Republicans, and where a Democrat hadn’t won statewide office in three decades — elected both a Democratic senator and a Democratic governor. Kansas now has its first Democratic senator since the Great Depression.

It will most likely take a few weeks to process the fallout. But at this point, the results are so stunning that many are seeing in this election not just a reckoning for Republicans, but a seismic shift in American politics: the beginning of the end of the Trump era.

A ‘stinging rebuke’

More than any of his predecessors, Trump tried to make the midterms a referendum on himself. He asked voters to “pretend I’m on the ballot,” not once or twice but 47 times.

They did. And they delivered what my colleague Peter Baker calls “a stinging rebuke” to a president who, after dominating the national stage for more than a decade, has become deeply unpopular.

The broad-based coalition that returned Trump to the White House in 2024, when he won over Latino men and doubled his support among Black voters, has collapsed. This chart by my colleagues shows every single American constituency swinging left.

There are many reasons for that. Americans are angry. Many told pollsters that they felt betrayed by Trump. He promised to end wars and bring down prices. Instead he started a war and sent prices at the gas pump soaring. He promised to “drain the swamp” and instead made more than $2 billion in his first year in office, helping propel voter concerns about corruption to heights they rarely reach.

And while many wanted him to close the border, they were uncomfortable with the heavy-handed ICE raids, the arrests targeting people who had been living in the country for years, and the deaths of multiple people, including U.S. citizens, in encounters with immigration officers.

The result: Despite eye-watering levels of pro-Trump campaign spending, despite multiple efforts by the Trump administration to interfere with voter rolls, and despite aggressive redistricting that tried to redraw the electoral map to favor Republicans, the Democrats’ margin of victory in the overall national vote for the House was about 13 percentage points. That’s the biggest win either party has lodged in a congressional election since at least 1976.

Checks and balances

As Peter points out, pundits have written Trump’s political obituary before, only to be proved wrong.

Still, something does seem different about this moment. Trump isn’t eligible to run for the presidency again. The scale of the wipeout has also hurt his credibility when it comes to selecting a successor: His handpicked candidates in some of the midterms’ most important races lost.

In other words, Trump’s power within his party has taken a hit. And Democrats are eager to use their new control of Congress to constrain him further. As my colleague Annie Karni recently explained, Democrats plan to use their oversight powers to investigate the administration on issues related to corruption, including the pardon industry that has emerged around Trump, and what Annie calls the “rivers of cryptocurrency” that are flowing into the government and the Trump family.

They’re also planning “a shock-and-awe legislative sprint,” with bills that, in addition to addressing domestic issues like health care funding, will try to scrap Trump’s tariffs and direct Trump to end the war in Iran.

On these last ambitions, though, they might only get so far. That’s the thing about lame ducks. Trump might be diminished — but he’s still commander in chief.

On domestic issues, Congress might be able to restrain Trump some. But when it comes to foreign policy, that’s harder. American presidents have enormous leeway to act alone. Some analysts have wondered whether Trump’s losses at home might even make him more inclined to make big moves overseas — including, perhaps, escalating the Iran war, now that he no longer has to worry about electoral consequences. Congress could try to exercise control — but its power to do so would be limited, as my colleague David Sanger explained this week.

If this is the beginning of the end of the Trump era, it won’t necessarily be stable or quiet. Donald Trump is president for another two years. And he is not known for going quietly.

Watch Peter Baker explain in the video below what makes these election results so striking.

Trump’s enemies and frenemies abroad did not hide their glee at the election results, with celebrations in Iran, China, South Africa and Brussels. Far-right leaders offered muted reactions.

“The reason we lost is the war,” said Vice President JD Vance, who is seen as a likely presidential candidate in 2028.

The U.S. stock market rallied, gaining more than 1 percent. Shares of Elon Musk’s companies, SpaceX and Tesla, both fell sharply.

item.title: On Cusp of Renewed War, More Iranians Are Calling for Nuclear Weapons
item.description:
From pulpits at Friday prayers to street rallies, Iranian clerics and officials are increasingly urging the country’s leaders to reverse their longtime pledge not to pursue nuclear weapons.

This demand, once seen as a fringe position held by hard-liners, is moving into mainstream public debate, and the shift could have dramatic consequences for Iran, whose government has for decades argued that its nuclear program was solely for peaceful purposes.

“We must be equipped with nuclear weapons — so that we can fight the criminal America with strength, God willing,” Ali Sepahvand, the Friday prayer leader in Iran’s western city of Kuhdasht, said last week, according to a widely distributed video.

As his voice echoed through a prayer hall, covered in photographs of commanders killed in the war with the United States and Israel this past year, the congregants chanted: “Nuclear deterrence is our inalienable right!”

The growing calls for Iran to pursue nuclear weapons come as the country’s leaders engage in diplomatic efforts to stave off renewed war with the United States and Israel, an outcome widely considered likely after the American midterm elections on Tuesday.

For decades, Iran’s officials have publicly endorsed the fatwa, or religious edict, from its supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, which forbade the development and use of nuclear weapons. Issued in his capacity as the head of Iran’s theocratic state, his decree barred Iranian institutions, including the military and Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, from pursuing a nuclear bomb.

Yet at the same time, Western intelligence agencies in past years reported signs Iran was enriching uranium to levels close to those that could be used to develop a bomb. Some officials in Israel and the United States accused Iran of preparing to build one, regardless of the fatwa.

To curb this threat, the United States and other world powers reached an agreement with Iran in 2015 to restrict its nuclear activities. Three years later, President Trump pulled out of that agreement.

Ayatollah Khamenei’s strategy, regional analysts say, had been to keep Iran’s nuclear intentions ambiguous in hopes of deterring attacks on Iran without it actually becoming a nuclear power.

But that approach failed to prevent the two wars Israel and the United States have waged against Iran since June 2025 — including the one in which Mr. Khamenei was himself killed in February.

“He created this neither in nor out situation, where they paid for a bomb they didn’t have,” said Mohammad Ali Shabani, an Iran analyst who edits the independent regional news site Amwaj.media. “Now, there is this sense that unless you have this ultimate weapon, you could end up at the mercy of not just the U.S., but Israel, at any point.”

President Trump’s own comments may strengthen this assessment, analysts say.

“If they had a nuclear weapon, I’d be calling the Supreme Leader and I’d be saying, ‘Mr. Supreme Leader, how are you, sir? Is there anything we can do for you?’ As opposed to bombing the crap out of him,” Mr. Trump said at the Republican midterm convention in September.

Inside Iran, calls for withdrawing from the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons, or N.P.T., which prohibits development of a nuclear weapon, have been growing ever since Israel and the United States attacked in 2025.

In recent weeks, an increasing number of Iranian political and religious figures have added their voices to this chorus, suggesting to some Iran analysts that there is an effort orchestrated, or at least enabled, by the country’s leadership.

It is unclear whether serious debate over Iran’s nuclear doctrine has reached the new supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei. But on Saturday, Iran’s top national security figure, Mohsen Rezaei, said in an interview on state television that Iran’s leaders were discussing it.

“No new decision has been made yet,” he said. “Of course, the debate now is whether we want to keep the same doctrine we had before the war, if war breaks out again.”

Advocating for withdrawal from the N.P.T. was once a minority position within Iran’s leadership, said Mohammad Ghaderi, a foreign affairs expert in Tehran.

Now, he argued, it is becoming a majority view. “They argue that if the military threats from the United States and Israel persist, withdrawing from the N.P.T. represents a crucial step toward establishing deterrence,” he said.

Raising the nuclear prospect at a time when Iran could be at the cusp of another possible attack by the United States or Israel may itself be a strategy, said Omid Memarian, an Iran analyst at DAWN, a Washington-based Middle East research group.

Mr. Rezaei’s entry into the debate, while Qatar has been leading intensive mediation efforts between Washington and Tehran, may be an attempt to push the United States to reach a deal, Mr. Memarian said.

“They are playing with this card: If the negotiation fails, we will seek a different path, and it will be costly for you,” he said.

Especially notable has been the number of Friday prayer leaders adding their voices to the calls and effectively challenging the late ayatollah’s fatwa.

“The taboo is gone,” said Mr. Shabani. “A religious foundation for the shift is here. The question is whether a strategic or political shift will follow.”

Some of Iran’s leading reformist figures, like the president Masoud Pezeshkian and former president Hassan Rouhani, continue to back Iran’s peaceful nuclear doctrine.

In Iran’s leading reformist newspaper, Shargh, a former diplomat, Kourosh Ahmadi, warned this week that abandoning that doctrine poses grave risks. The plethora of pro-weapon statements from prominent figures, he said, “is dangerous because it makes the work of officials trying to prevent another war more difficult.”

And until Iran could manage to build a bomb, he argued, the chances of being attacked would actually increase.

After U.S. and Israeli strikes wiped out most of Iran’s top leadership and battered its infrastructure, it is harder for critics of the nuclear option to make their case, said Sina Toossi, an Iran expert at the Center for International Policy, a Washington-based think tank.

“The central problem for advocates of restraint is explaining what Iran gained from remaining below the nuclear threshold,” he said.

At the same time, he said, a new round of U.S. attacks “could strengthen the very arguments for the nuclear weapons that Washington says it wants to prevent.”

At public prayers in Tehran on Friday, the prayer leader, Mohammad Javad Haj Ali Akbari, declared that changing Iran’s nuclear doctrine was “a national demand,” according to a video posted on social media.

His congregants immediately responded with a refrain common at government-sponsored rallies from decades past: “Nuclear energy is our inalienable right!”

“This is an old slogan,” he told them, and smiled: “We have gone way beyond that.”

Leily Nikounazar and Sanam Mahoozi contributed reporting

item.title: This Grandma Believes She Can Fix Africa’s Richest City
item.description:
To the beat of a Zulu rap song, the polished, 1990s-era BMW convertible rolled into the political rally in Johannesburg, greeted by delirious cheers from hundreds of South Africans. The car, known as a “gusheshe,” became synonymous with the hip culture that emerged from the largely impoverished townships where Black people were forced to live under apartheid.

But sitting atop the gusheshe (pronounced GOO-shay-shay) was someone South Africans may hardly associate with Black culture. It was Helen Zille, 75, a white grandmother who has been criticized for her stances on race, including past statements suggesting that colonialism had its benefits, denouncing affirmative action in South Africa and embracing American right-wing terms like “wokeness.”

Yet, as she campaigns to lead South Africa’s largest city, Johannesburg, ahead of Wednesday’s election, Ms. Zille is betting that race no longer guides many South Africans’ decisions in the voting booth.

Instead, she argues, South Africans are more concerned with quality-of-life issues like water shortages, crumbling roads and public safety. And her blunt, rugged style, she says, is best suited to getting Africa’s wealthiest city working again.

With an outsize persona and social media outreach that feels more Gen Z than baby boomer, Ms. Zille has injected excitement, and some controversy, into the typically bland, predictable ritual of South African electioneering.

“Lots of people don’t like me,” Ms. Zille, the mayoral candidate for the Democratic Alliance, or D.A., said in an interview. “It’s fine. You don’t even have to like the D.A. You just have to love Johannesburg to consolidate your vote behind us.”

Ms. Zille’s strategy has put her ahead in the polls in Johannesburg, the biggest prize in an election in which millions of voters are expected to choose mayors and city councilors across the nation. The local elections could have important repercussions for the national political landscape, analysts said.

The African National Congress, the party of Nelson Mandela that led South Africa out of apartheid, has experienced a sharp electoral decline. In the country’s past two major elections, less than half of South Africa’s voters chose the A.N.C., an unheard-of development for the party since it came to power after apartheid ended in 1994.

Polls and analysts suggest an even further slide is coming this election, with the A.N.C. projected to be surpassed as the largest party in most of South Africa’s eight major metropolitan cities. (It’s currently the largest in six of them.) The A.N.C.’s diminution could deepen fighting within the party, experts say, and intensify tensions in the national government coalition led by the A.N.C. The party could also be forced to moderate its policy ambitions and accede to some of its rivals’ demands.

Most metro areas in South Africa are not projected to have clear-cut winners in the election, raising fears among some analysts that parties will form unstable governing coalitions that will make life harder for ordinary South Africans.

“I’m really pessimistic about the future of this country,” said Bheki Mngomezulu, a political science professor at Nelson Mandela University.

Historically, the A.N.C. had not announced mayoral candidates before elections, instead relying on its brand to attract voters. This year, with Ms. Zille’s popularity presenting a possible threat, the A.N.C. broke with tradition and announced three finalists for its mayoral candidate in Johannesburg, a sprawling city of nearly five million people.

But the party bungled that effort when its leadership failed to formally submit the name of one of those finalists, Frank Chikane, to the electoral commission. That means he is currently not eligible to become mayor.

The A.N.C. has turned to Cyril Ramaphosa, South Africa’s president and the party’s leader, in an effort to defy the grim projections about how it will fare in the elections. He is the party’s most respected figure.

Mr. Ramaphosa has been barnstorming the country trying to persuade voters to stick with the party. Last month, he waded through crowds in the township of Soweto, speaking with voters complaining that they lacked water, electricity and jobs.

“When you do the balance, when you look at the balance sheet, there’s more positive than negative,” Mr. Ramaphosa told a crowd gathered on the street, referring to the A.N.C.’s governing record.

In South Africa, voters select parties that then form coalitions to pick the mayor. About 80 parties are competing in Johannesburg. But Ms. Zille is polling way ahead of other candidates, though still less than the 50 percent needed to become mayor outright.

Her campaign has been hyper-focused on making the A.N.C.’s governing failures go viral.

She has posted to social media videos of her “snorkeling” in a huge pothole filled with water from a burst pipe; paddling an inflatable boat in flooded Soweto streets; and directing traffic at a broken traffic light. She conducted an unannounced “oversight” visit to a crumbling, abandoned municipal building, unveiling a dramatic video that included being chased by security guards.

Shortly before the political rally last month in which she rode on the back of the convertible, she posted a video of herself screeching a gusheshe in circles, kicking up smoke and leaving skid marks. Spinning cars is a popular activity in South African townships.

“Other parties will spin you stories,” she said into the camera. “We’ll spin into action.”

The comments section lit up with laughing emojis, clapping hands, flames and praise for “Gogo Helen.” (Gogo is the term used for grandmother in Black communities.)

“You know what, take my vote,” one commenter wrote.

Critics, though, have accused Ms. Zille of pandering to Black communities by reaching for caricatures and stereotypes. Some have called her stunts gimmicks that avoid the hard work of engaging Black voters.

And Dada Morero, the current mayor of Johannesburg and a member of the A.N.C., has criticized the D.A. for fomenting inequalities in the cities it has governed and cast doubt on Ms. Zille’s commitment to Johannesburg.

“This sudden interest in Johannesburg by the D.A. is not about residents; it is about politics,” he told a South African news outlet in response to one of Ms. Zille’s viral social media posts.

Most public polls have Ms. Zille shy of 40 percent of the vote, a tally that may make it difficult for her to pull together a coalition of parties to become Johannesburg’s next mayor. But some analysts say her path to office could run through a coalition with the A.N.C., which the D.A. is already partnering with in the national government.

Before entering political office in the late 1990s, Ms. Zille was a journalist for a newspaper that was critical of the apartheid regime. She famously debunked the apartheid government’s claim that the activist Steve Biko had died from the effects of a hunger strike. Her investigation found that he had sustained extensive brain damage and bruising, suggesting that he had been killed in police custody.

In 2007, Ms. Zille became the mayor of Cape Town, South Africa’s second-largest city, and she later served a decade as the premier of Western Cape Province. It seemed as if Ms. Zille’s political career was approaching its twilight last year, when, as a top D.A. official, she was tasked with leading the party’s selection of a Johannesburg mayoral candidate.

She surveyed the field, she said, and thought about her own experience in cutthroat municipal politics.

“People get killed here, and you are always being attacked and then your name gets dragged through the mud on social media and in mainstream media,” she said. “So it’s not a job that many people want.”

Ms. Zille found that the party “didn’t have anyone who could quite rise to that,” she said.

It struck her, she said, that as a woman whose aunt lived to 104 and whose mother smoked but made it to 95, she had a lot left to give.

So she threw her hat into the ring.
